utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. The Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's urgent motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with five additional exhibits. I would like to ask the Defence if you are in a position to respond to this motion orally. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection to the Prosecution's request to amend their 65 ter exhibit list with the five additional exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We noticed, Mr. McCloskey, that we have now three different procedures to amend the 65 ter exhibit list. One is by a little star in the list of documents to be used with a witness and with a note, "with the leave of the Chamber." The second is without any comment. And the third is -- the second was to -- a motion submitted orally. And the third is now in written form. I think for the future it would be sufficient just to address the Chamber orally in court. It's not necessary to file a written motion of that kind. The Chamber will consider this present motion. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the motion and grants leave to add these five documents to the 65 ter exhibit list. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone. Yes, thank you for clarifying the procedure. I had a little extra time so we did it that way, but it's much -- I think it's much better the way you've noted, especially for documents like this that were part of the testimony of this witness before. The witness is ready. And I would ask that the witness be given a caution, if you could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness should be brought into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, and, Mr. President, we do -- this witness is celebrating his -- the -- the memoriam of his mother's death beginning on Saturday and so that's obviously a very important family event, and so we should -- we should have plenty of time under the guide-lines, but I just wanted to inform you of that. We hope to get him travelling on Friday. But I think it looks like we should be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to give you a caution. You know in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90, we have a specific rule about this caution and I would like to read out paragraph (E) of Rule 90. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand what I was reading to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey is now commencing his examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I am Ljubomir Obradovic. I was born on the 30th of January, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In Visegrad, I believe.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you were -- you've been here before; you were called as a Defence witness in the Miletic trial a few years back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to listen to your testimony in that trial and review the exhibits that were shown to you in that trial by both sides?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same sorts of questions, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And is it fair to say that, as you -- you grew up in Bosnia, you went on to be a career military officer, first with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us -- let's get to the period when the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina starts, in the spring of 1992. Can you tell us, did you -- what your position was when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was stationed in the Derventa garrison. I was the Chief of Staff of the 327th Motorised Brigade. And I was acting as the commander of the brigade, which means that I was, at that time, performing both functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And throughout the period of 1992 and 1993, did you retain that position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what corps that brigade was in? Derventa is not a town that we here much about in this case.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The 327th Motorised Brigade was within the 17 Corps of the JNA. After some officers left the brigade for Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, and Montenegro, it was mostly the Serb officers from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina who stayed, voluntarily. Not all of them but most of them stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that brigade became part of the VRS during 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the name of the brigade in the VRS scheme?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It changed its name during the war. It used to be the 327th Infantry Brigade, and it also used to be called the 27th Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which of the corps of the VRS was it in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After the reorganisation and after the East Bosnian Corps of the VRS was formed, this brigade was within the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your position in 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994 I was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of -- of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did they finally bring in a commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in 1994 were you transferred to another responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of September, 1994, I received the order which transferred me into the Main Staff of the VRS, where I was the chief of the operative detachment in the operations and training administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your rank when you first came to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your duty station the -- the base at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at some point were you assigned to go out into the field under General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My first assignment was two or three days after I arrived. I went with the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, General Tolimir, and Colonel Magazin to the Panorama hotel in Pale. We had a meeting with the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR. I think his name was Briquemont.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe, just very briefly, your basic assignments, whether it was at Crna Rijeka or out in the field.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As the chief of the operative department, my job was to follow the operative situation and the situation in the battlefield, also to write orders, warnings, reports, plans. And I also had to follow the operative log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'll get into a little more detail on what your actual job was. Right now I just want to get whether or not you went out into the field on any lengthy field assignments after you were first assigned to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In mid-November 1994, after the offensive of the 5th Muslim Corps, in the area of Bihac, which was directed towards Krupa and Donji Vakuf, the commander of the Main Staff decided to establish a forward command post of the Main Staff in order to stabilize the front in that area. General Milovanovic was sent to perform that task together with a certain number of officers, and that was in the second half of October 1994. After about a month, he requested to be sent an operative man by the chief of administration and that operative man was me, so I went to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. At some point during the war, was your brother taken prisoner in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was he able to be exchanged or released?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the negotiations, the Muslim side procrastinated. And whichever variant of the exchange there was, my brother was always the last on the list to be exchanged. He was exchanged after almost two years, two years less ten days. He was captured on the 16th of October, 1992, and he was exchanged on the 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you tell me a short time ago that General Tolimir assisted in -- in getting your brother exchanged?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir frequently went to meetings with Professor Koljevic. He tried to make the exchange agreement on the principle all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so did he, in your view, assist in getting your brother released? General Tolimir, that is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. My brother and all others who were exchanged during the period that he was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you very briefly tell us who Koljevic is? You mentioned his name, that General Tolimir went with him. Just, who was he, what was his position? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic was, if I'm not mistaken, the vice-president of Republika Srpska. The second vice-president was Biljana Plavsic. He was involved in humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at some point while you were on this field assignment, did you break your leg?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I broke a leg in Jasenica on the 27th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said that was on the ice.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go to recover from that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the clinical centre in Banja Luka. I was treated there and then, later on, I was transferred to my place of residence in Derventa. After the initial treatment, they put the blaster on, in Doboj, and then all the rest of that time I spent in Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you next go when you got better?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After my sick-leave, I returned to the Main Staff on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you promoted to colonel in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what position did you go back to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I went back to my previous position, which was the chief of the operative department within the operative -- operations and training administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm sure you recall testifying about the -- some of the formations and structures of the -- of the Main Staff from your previous testimony. And were you able to just make a rough drawing of some of those positions from your memory for me a day or two ago?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 7295. And, Your Honours, this is not designed to be an exact replica of the rough drawing that the witness gave us, but it's -- it's roughly similar. And if I could just hand him his rough drawing. It's a big document, so it's hard to get a feel for it. As you can see, it's hard to see from the screen. And if I could hand him this so he just has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we -- is it possible to have that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I actually have hard copies for Your Honours and -- and I've given hard copies to the -- to the General and Mr. Gajic of -- of his diagram. And I have hard copies of the English. But, of course, it's also possible to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be -- it's not necessary if we can receive a hard copy of that, and the Defence. The Court Usher will assist you. Mr. Gajic and Mr. Tolimir indicate that they have the drawing but not the English version of it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're passing over the English -- the English version of it over to Mr. Gajic. So as I say, it's not exact. It's not meant to be exact. But we tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you help me. We received now a printed version. Is this exactly the printed version of the hand drawing of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. It is based on that. But this was a rather rough item that he did and some of the positions he told us about but didn't draw them in, and one of the positions he -- he just mentioned to me yesterday that he had forgotten. So we had -- we've tried to make this to be a reflection of it, but it's really just meant to be a testimonial guide at this point, with the witness's help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to understand your -- your procedure now. The witness has a copy of his hand -- the sketch he drawed. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the Defence is in possession of that as well; yes? Do we have hard copies for the Chamber of that hand drawing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have some extras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would assist us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- to understand your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Cyrillic. I don't know how good your Cyrillic's getting. Mine has never gotten very good, but ... This is -- it's really, Your Honour and -- Mr. President, Your Honours, I wanted you to first see the whole team, as it were, and then we'll zero in on the different units, and that's mostly what I'm concerned about, is not so much the structure diagram at this -- at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General Obradovic, the diagram you did, it roughly has the -- the commander, the Chief of Staff, the assistant commanders of the various branches, and the corps, and a few other units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was your memory of -- of the important parts of the Main Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you know, we -- we put in the corner, you can probably see it in the English, the 67th Communications Regiment that you had mentioned to me yesterday. Where does that connect to? We didn't put any connecting line to it. But who -- where do they fit into the unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The 67th Communications Regiment is a unit attached to the staff. In this case, the Main Staff. Its main task is to organise the communications, to satisfy the communications needs of the Main Staff. It is attached to the commander. In performing its professional duties, it is attached to the arms within the staff sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And while we're on that, I might as well just -- you're referring to the staff sector that's the Chief of Staff and deputy commander General Milovanovic is noted in the diagram; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that. But let's start with just a brief explanation for us of the commander, Ratko Mladic. Can you -- can you just tell us, in the most fundamental form, what is his position as the commander of the Main Staff and his basic duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff commands the Army of Republika Srpska and institutions through the commands of units and institutions. It is his task to take care of the organisation and the building of combat readiness of the entire army. He commands by issuing directives, orders, instructions, warnings, advice, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let me ask you: The next person, the deputy commander, Chief of Staff, was that General Milovanovic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, General Milovanovic was the Chief of Staff and deputy commander throughout the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Milovanovic was chief of the staff sector all the time. And due to the -- his position in the establishment, he was at the same time commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that should be Chief of Staff but at the same time deputy commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Chief of Staff. The sector that he immediately was in charge of was the staff sector, and, simultaneously, he was deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's -- that's important. Can you -- can you tell us how that job worked? What was the difference, just fundamentally, between his position as deputy commander and position as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff does operative work, work concerning the services of the armed forces, and he has subordinate units that are in charge of these kinds of work. He -- he organises the work of the commands of the Main Staff by planning, monitoring the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He's deputy commander if the commander himself should be absent for any period of time. Then he takes over during the commander's absence but can only issue orders in the spirit of the directives and decisions that had previously been passed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how was the term "absent" defined? We -- for example, we see General Mladic going to Serbia, going to Belgrade. Would that be considered an absence or would he still be the commander in full command and Milovanovic would still be Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He would temporarily stand in for the commander during the commander's absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would going to Serbia be considered absent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't depend on the whereabouts of the commander but it depends on the duration of absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were at Main Staff in 1995, were you aware of Mladic being absent, where someone else had to be the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I personally do not know. When the commander goes somewhere, he appoints one of his assistants to stand in for him during his absence. And his assistants were, apart from General Milovanovic, the chief of the morale, religious, and legal affairs; the chief of the logistics sector; the chief of the organisational, mobilisation, and personnel issues; then the chief of the intelligence and security sector; then the chief of the planning, development, and finance administration; and the chief of the air force and anti-aircraft defence administration. These persons are the assistants of the commander of the Main Staff and they are directly organisationally linked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us, was General Tolimir an assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which branch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence and security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Gvero, which branch?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero was chief of the morale, religious, and legal affairs sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Skrbic was chief of the organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The late General Djukic was chief of the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Jovo Maric?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The late Jovo Maric was chief of the air force and air defence administration. He was a pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain briefly and -- in 1995, as best you can recall, just how did General Milovanovic interact with the assistant commanders and the -- the -- the staff sector? Can you just give us just a rough idea of how that worked.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was at the forward command post for a significant part of 1995, that is, outside of Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: While I was there, it was Jasenica. That is south-west of the town of Krupa on the Una River. After that, there was an opportunity, while I was still there, so that we moved on to Drvar from the forward command post because of some other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And during the time-period when General Milovanovic was at the Main Staff, both in 1995 and in 1994 when you were working there, can you just describe basically his duties and how he interacted with the assistant commanders. You've described briefly about his position over the staff, but what was his authority over the assistant commanders or -- and his dealings with them? Just briefly. He'll be here to testify, we hope, and we'll get into more detail about that. But if we could just get a rough guide line from you, it will help your testimony, I think.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: We must distinguish his work in the staff sector from the jobs that he did in the command of the Main Staff. In the staff sector, there was a training and operations administration, an organ for the services. Then a data processing organ. There was an office. And there was a typists' bureau. In the operations and training administration, there was a department for operative work headed by me. There was a department for training headed by Colonel Krsto Djeric. And the operations centre wasn't manned. We were not able to establish it the way it was supposed to be. General Milovanovic, in the staff sector, co-ordinated the work of the administrations organs, services, offices, and the part that belongs to the staff sector, according to the establishment; whereas, in the Main Staff, he co-ordinated the work of the individual sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, I have a -- a note that there is under the staff sector something called a combat services, where the chief of engineering, chief of artillery, and the armoured units and the chief of communications are placed; are they also within the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: They, all together, that is, the chief of infantry, chief of artillery, chief of armoured and mechanized units, chief of communications, chief of ABC defence, they all belonged to the staff sector. And the joint name for all these together is the services organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you had mentioned, you described the work that General Milovanovic did related to the staff sector. And then you ended by saying he co-ordinated the work of the individual sectors. And can you tell us what sectors you're talking about and what this coordination was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the individual sectors, but he co-ordinated the sectors themselves; that is, the coordination was between the sectors. Because, if I may say, the functions of commanding are planning, organisation, giving orders, coordination, and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so can you remind us, there may be slight translation issues, what are the sectors we're talking about? If you could just remind us, to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: There's the sector for morale; the logistics sector; intelligence and security; organisational, mobilisation, and personnel affairs. And then there are the administrations: Planning, development, and finance, as well as air force and air defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Those are the assistant commanders that you spoke of earlier. So he coordinates the work of the assistant commanders, their sectors.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example or just describe to us briefly what this command function of coordination would entail?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Coordination means the harmonized work of sectors. It can mean the work in the field among units that are at the same level. None is superior or subordinate to the other, and somebody should coordinate that; whereas, it's the Chief of Staff who coordinates the work of the sectors, when they perform the same task at the same time. For example, Directive 7/1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We'll get to that but -- so don't get into too much detail because I'm going to want the Court to see that and all when we get to it. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I only wanted to add to make -- something to make things clearer. If a task is supposed to be carried out by forces of three corps in the same area, such as the East Bosnia Corps, the Drina Corps, and the -- another corps, then somebody must coordinate, which means that either a temporary command must be established which will be superior to the forces of all three corps and whose orders will be carried out by the commanders of all these corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as an example of the coordination within the Main Staff, you have mentioned the directives. And we'll -- we're going to get to those directives soon, and we'll use that as an example and just save that for now and so we don't have to back-track. So, all right. Now let's -- let's go to General Miletic. We see that he is the -- in the administration for operations and training. So where does he fit into -- into this staff that you're part of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He's in the staff at the head of the administration for operations and training. Subordinate to him there was the department for operations, then the department for training and the training centre. But the training centre never took off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what subordinates, if any, did General Miletic have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Gajic, please. One moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 18, line 16, a training centre is mentioned. I believe that the witness said something else. Could Mr. McCloskey please clarify this. It's about a centre that never took off the ground, but I believe that I heard something else, something other than what's recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mean in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. In the language spoken by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. General, can you clarify, what was this centre that you said never got off the ground?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: An integral part of the administration according to the establishment was the operations department headed by me, and I -- I was also Miletic's deputy. There was a cartographer in that department too, a Lieutenant Micanovic. But actually many more people were required than the two of us, but we weren't manned. Then it was Colonel Djeric who was chief of the training department and then nobody else. And the third unit is the operations centre, which was envisaged as consisting of a chief, two higher-ranking officers, such as a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, who could be shift leaders there. But these positions weren't manned, and we didn't have an operations centre but only an operative duty officer in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it was the operations centre that never got off the ground?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you said it was envisioned to have a certain number of posts or position. Can you tell us a bit about that? It was envisioned by who? And what military organisation envisions or would have signed the normal number of posts for something like this? Who's doing the overall design of -- of this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs sector, there's a department for formations, and it was tasked with forming formations. Somebody envisaged the formation of the Main Staff. I believe that the leadership of the republic appointed Mladic commander of the Main Staff and that it was he who organised at least the inner circle of his associates from the personnel available, and they were chiefs of sectors. The chiefs of sectors, probably, once officers become available, they propose some persons for individual positions which is then approved by the collegium of the Main Staff, because that body is responsible for appointments, that is, for confirming appointments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now -- I think now it's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under this design, how many people were envisioned to actually work in the administration for operations and training?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The operations and training administration headed by General Miletic was supposed to have 18 officers, according to the establishment, but there were only four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you have named Djeric as the sector for training. You were the chief of the --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the department, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have one other on your list who was a cartographer as your fourth; who's that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Micanovic. He's not a cryptographer. He's a cartographer. It was Lieutenant Micanovic. He graduated from military academy the -- and he was a trained surveyor. He drew maps and made the topographic material that we used to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I won't ask you about who the 14 other positions were that were envisioned, but we can see that that -- it was envisioned to have a lot more than your four. Was that low manning level typical throughout the different sectors of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that any one was fully manned. I cannot be more precise than that though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was General Miletic. Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall I asked you at the last trial that when you drafted documents in -- pursuant to your position, were you responsible for those documents?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My responsibility was to produce documents conscientiously, and it's the superior officer's responsibility to review it and, if it's all right, sign it or possibly forward it to his commander to sign, depending on the type of enactment or document. So it was my responsibility to do my job conscientiously, but the one who's legally responsible is the one who signs the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Miletic was responsible for the documents that you did for him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as your immediate superior, was he responsible for your work, be it at the Crna Rijeka or out in the field, if you went out in the field?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every superior has that responsibility, the responsibility to monitor the work of their subordinates, to assess the quality of their work and the work they put in to accomplishing their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've used the term "monitor." Can you tell us, is -- what does that mean in the sense of a superior/subordinate? Can you give a -- describe to it a little more? Because we have -- you may recall there was questions regarding following someone's work and monitoring someone's work. Can you tell us what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's one and the same or would be one and the same if we are talking about the daily tasks. On a daily basis, a superior has to follow the work of their subordinates. When they give them a task, then they have to monitor how the task was carried out, whether that person was skillful, whether the task was carried out conscientiously or whether it was carried out superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you were given a task by, for example, Milovanovic when Miletic was absent, would you be reporting back to General Miletic, and would he be monitoring your work even though Milovanovic had given you the order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In practice, when the second in command issues a task, I proceed to carry the task out, but I have to report to my immediate superior as to what kind of task I had been given by the second in command or the second superior. There were lots of problems with writing reports. For example, General Milanovic [as interpreted] wanted me to give him reports, bypassing General Miletic. And the other officers were the same. They were not subordinated to Miletic. In other words, General Milovanovic would be the one to inspect such reports and sign them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did you go through Miletic as the -- what you've identified as the proper order, proper chain of following those orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: However, if he was not present physically and if priority and speed were required, then I would go directly to the person who had issued the order in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you started your answer with yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when he is present. However, if he is absent, then I could not give a report to him to inspect, and it was required from me to submit it immediately. But I would, nevertheless, inform him about the tasks that I had been given and that I have carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how -- normally how soon would you have to inform Miletic in such a situation where he wasn't immediately available? I mean, was it important to inform him as soon as possible? Could you wait? What -- how did that work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Usually those tasks were not that urgent. I would only inform him about what had happened during his absence, what tasks and duties had been carried out and on whose request. There were no tasks for which we would have had to report to him immediately without any delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were, as you've testified earlier, you were sent to the forward command post with -- the Main Staff forward command post with General Milovanovic, did you have any responsibilities to report back to General Miletic when you were in that forward command post? I think that was over in the ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Not regularly. But we did speak to each other at certain intervals and we exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you still responsible to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was responsible to him in general terms. More specifically, when it comes to my work at the forward command post, I was responsible to General Milanovic [as interpreted], because there I also worked as an operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify the last name. I heard Milanovic in the interpretation but it is written General "Milovanovic" in the transcript. Please clarify with the witness what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you clarify who you said you were working under? Which -- just the name. We didn't quite catch the name. When you were out at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: At the IKM, Your Honours, at the IKM, whatever I had to do at the IKM I received my tasks from General Milovanovic. In general terms, my immediate superior who was responsible for my overall work was General Miletic, but he was not there. He was in Crna Rijeka at the main command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did he remain, in general terms, responsible for your work as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the one who evaluated my work, who followed my work, who was responsible for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that, just so we can try to understand. The military is perhaps different from the rest of the world. How is it that a -- General Miletic -- well, how is it a subordinate is so responsible -- or the superior is so responsible for the work of the subordinate?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the doctrines of militaries and Warsaw Pact, this is very pronounced. There is less independence in decision-making at lower levels than was the case in our military, according to our doctrine documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go briefly over to the -- General Gvero's sector: Morale, legal, and religious. Do you remember any subordinates that he had working under him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I know people who were there, but I don't know what positions they had been appointed to. I wouldn't go into that. That sector had a department for morale and religious affairs, a department for information, and a department for legal affairs. In the legal affairs department, there was Lieutenant-Colonel Supic. As for the information department and department for religious affairs, whether Colonel Savo Sokanovic was there ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was General Gvero responsible for the work of those subordinates as you have described Miletic was responsible for your work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the intelligence and security affairs, you have noted two different administrations. Can you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration and the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the intelligence administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura. Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Ljubisa or Ljubo Beara. I don't know what his real name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was General Tolimir responsible for the work of those two people as General Miletic was responsible for your work and General Gvero was responsible for the work of his people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Tolimir was the chief of the sector for intelligence and security. That was made up of the two administrations that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've mentioned briefly about the Main Staff forward command post. Can you tell us what the purpose of -- of that was, why the Main Staff would have its own forward command post in some of these operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Forward command posts are formed with a view to establishing a more immediate contact and with a view to having ability to monitor combat operations and exert influence on the course of those combat activities. The area in question was covered by two corps. There had to be coordination in that part of the front and an opportunity had to be given to the Main Staff to exert a more immediate influence on the course of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why not rely on the -- the corps or the brigade forward command post? Why create a Main Staff forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The area where the events were taking place was not suitable for organising a forward command post, either of the 1st or the 2nd Corps, because they were too far from each other. In principle, when things like that are organised, an IKM of a superior unit can be an IKM of a subordinated unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did General Mladic prefer having a Main Staff officer involved in operations when it was possible? I mean, you obviously talked about Milovanovic on that very important front. Is that something General Mladic did on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When General Milovanovic went on field missions, that was done on the order of the commander. When operations are carried out involving several different corps, then a forward command post is established to coordinate the work and to carry out uniformed command in such operations. There were cases when the commander sent officers from the Main Staff to certain areas, when some extraordinary situations occurred, when positions were lost, when there was -- desertion. That was done to help a subordinated command or this was done to satisfy the function of control on behalf of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to go to another area that you had spent some time talking about. And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I would like to put a question to the witness to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- more correctly your description of the sector headed by Manojlo Milovanovic. You told us that General Miletic was the administration chief for operations and training and you have been his deputy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about the other three officers? I would like to know the level of their posts and the relation to General Miletic and, if there was, a relation to you. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By establishment, the chief of operations was also the deputy of the administration. And the second organisational unit was the department for education and training. Colonel Krsto Djeric was in charge of that. And the third unit was the operations centre, for which we did not have an officer because it was simply not organised. In my department, we had Lieutenant Micanovic who was a cartographer, together with some desk officers who were supposed to be members of the department that I worked in by formation -- by establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was the direct superior of Colonel Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was he also a deputy of General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But establishment, the chief of the operations department was also General Miletic's deputy, the chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey. Sorry, Judge Mindua has another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Before you remove this chart, I would like to know the following. Witness, I followed, of course, with great attention your testimony concerning various functions of the Main Staff personnel, VRS structure Main Staff. But I do have one concern regarding various ranks and the way they're called. Because, as you know, of course, in every country, the hierarchy of these ranks are very important. And, of course, it's always important that these ranks correspond with the functions of officers. But I noticed that in many documents that we see there's a great confusion, according to me, with respect to the way the ranks are called. Maybe it's just a matter of translation or interpretation. I can just imagine how confusing that can be. But if we look at this chart, 65 ter 7295, titled: "Main Staff VRS Structure July 1995," it would seem to me that there's also this -- the same confusion is also there. We see, for instance, commander Ratko Mladic, and his rank is lieutenant-colonel general; right? Because I'm trying to translate into French for myself. And it would seem that his deputy would be Manojlo Milovanovic. But he had the -- he has the same rank; he's also a lieutenant-colonel general. Now, that can happen, I understand. It's not really a problem. However, the subordinate of Milovanovic, whose name is Radivoje Miletic, his rank is -- is the rank of a -- he is a general. So to me that is a bit strange. Is it possible at all? I can also notice that the assistant commander was Zdravko Tolimir, and he also bore the same rank, the rank of a general. And we're in July 1995. While his superior bears the rank of lieutenant-general, whereas we know that lieutenant -- that Mr. Tolimir was a lieutenant-general during the period -- major-general, rather. So I would like to know, since you belonged to a category of superior officers, I would like to know what was the rank between the general officers of the VRS? What was the hierarchy in July of 1995? So going from the smallest general up to the highest general, what was the hierarchy and what were these ranks called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was the situation then. General Mladic became a lieutenant-colonel thereafter. However, it was not just the ranks that matter but also the positions. And our rule -- rules allowed for the officers sharing the same rank to occupy positions either of a superior or subordinate. I don't see a problem here. For a while I was the chief of the operations department as a lieutenant-colonel. And then, at the same time, Colonel Krsto Djeric was the head of a different department. Still I was Colonel Miletic's deputy. And Colonel Miletic became a general in June when I became a colonel. Those were our conditions at the time. Those officers who volunteered, because they hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were assigned to various positions based on their educational background and inclinations. The fact that they didn't have the same ranks or perhaps had the same rank and were subordinated to each other doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... very much. Thanks, yes, I understand. But let's go back to this chart that we have before us. In July of 1995, what did this rank of Ratko Mladic mean, lieutenant-colonel general? So if compare this rank to -- to Mr. Tolimir, who is superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake here. General Tolimir, that's like a general term, but he was major-general. So would be lower in rank than lieutenant-colonel. But the word "major" is missing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Witness. So in July of 1995, according to this chart as we see it here, it's actually not exactly correct when it comes to the ranks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that statement correct? That was a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I was asking the question. I put the question to the witness. So I wanted to know if this structure of the Main Staff of the VRS in July of 1995, is it incorrect according to the way the ranks are written here. Is it -- is it false? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The people's name are correct, but their ranks are not complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And thank you. I think it's probably a good idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's try to fix this. So can you tell us, if you can recall, and if you can't, don't worry about it, General Milovanovic, was he a lieutenant-colonel general in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in July 1995, what was General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In July he was major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've already clarified that General Tolimir was a major-general. How about Gvero? Is Gvero lieutenant general -- sorry, Lieutenant-Colonel General Gvero, as we have here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that is what we have here, okay. How about Skrbic? Do you recall what his --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about the late Djukic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Djukic was lieutenant-colonel general. He was the oldest among all these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about Jovo Maric?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Tomic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on that similar point, when you were a lieutenant-colonel working as Miletic's deputy, could you -- were you superior to Colonel Djeric?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. By position, I was his superior, although my rank was lower. And that was before July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you, if you were acting as Miletic's deputy, issue an order to Djeric even though you weren't equal to his rank?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My establishment post was the chief of the operations department and at the same time the deputy of the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The chief of the administration, the interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question from me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is: Do you know if General Tolimir had a deputy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Don't know whom he appointed to deputize for him, when he was absent, of the two chiefs of administrations. I don't know who it would have been by establishment. You would have to consult the establishment papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put an additional question. And then again Judge Mindua. What was your rank in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the rank of Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I thank you because now we do have the complete names of the various officers' ranks in the chart. But you forgot to answer one of my questions. I was asking you what was the hierarchy of the general officers' ranks within the BSA? Because in French we have "général de brigade," which is major-general, which is the lowest rank. Then we have the colonel general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter: lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then the -- which is, in French, "général de corps d'armée." And then we have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: -- word which is, in French, "général d'armée." I'd like to have the corresponding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] -- of ranks, the lowest would be major-general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to stop you because we lost most of the record. I think there was a problem with the interpretation channel. The last question of Judge Mindua is not correctly recorded. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I resume my question because I hope this will be of help for us in the future part of your testimony, in order to better understand the ranks within the BSA. So I was saying that, Witness, you had not answered one of my questions, which was related to the hierarchy of the various general staff generals' ranks within the BSA, and I did compare these ranks with the French ranks, French army ranks. As far as France is concerned, at the lowest level we have the "général de brigade," brigadiers. Then above him we have the "général de division," major-general. Above him the lieutenant-general, "général de corps d'armée," and above him the colonel general, "général d'armée." Could you help us, please, and give us the corresponding ranks in the BSA. And I hope that with the help of the French interpreters I will be able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Republika Srpska adopted the organisation and the rules of service from the JNA. In the JNA, the ranks of general follow the -- the following hierarchy: major-general, lieutenant-colonel general, colonel general. In the former state and in the former military, there was also the rank of a general of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is very clear now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it in the VRS you had three ranks of generals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the answer page 35, line 6, the -- the witness said we had "the following hierarchy: major-general, lieutenant-colonel general, and colonel general." And only in the former Yugoslavian army --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you had army -- general of the army; is that correct? In the VRS you didn't have such a rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think now we have it quite clear and a common understanding of the ranks. We are over time now. We must have our first break. And we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00. Before we leave the courtroom, I would like to come back to a request of the Prosecution of yesterday. We were asked to sit in the morning of the -- of Tuesday -- no, sorry, of Thursday this week. And the Defence was in agreement with that. The Chamber is also fine with the movement to the morning on Tuesday this week. Again, on Thursday. Thank you. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I realized I do need to stay with this chart a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you -- can you tell us, have you heard of a unit called the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where it fit in the hierarchy or where it was attached to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Like all other units from the first to the Herzegovina Corps, the units attached to the staff and the 10th Sabotage Detachment were under the command of the commander. While professionally speaking, they were, in a certain sense, subordinated to the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This will be a term we'll hear more of. Can you explain to the Court what you mean when you say "professionally speaking"; "along this professional line." What does that mean as -- in relation to this 10th being connected to the intelligence administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the full name was Reconnaissance Sabotage Detachment. And because of that reconnaissance tasks, it was attached through the professional line to the intelligence administration. Similarly, the communications regiment was professionally attached to the staff, because the staff contained the communications organ, which commanded and controlled, professionally speaking, those units who were in charge of organising the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you distinguish for us just perhaps a little bit more. We now understand that the 10th Sabotage Detachment is under the command of the commander Mladic, like the corps are, like the other places. That's -- that's clear. And now you say it's -- but it's professionally under the control of the intelligence administration. What is it -- what do you mean by that? How can this -- can it be under two -- two authorities at once?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This second jurisdiction does not entail the power to issue orders. The intelligence administration follows the training and the materiel empowerment of the reconnaissance units. That's the professional line. However, the line of issuing orders goes along the line of subordination, which means from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the intelligence administration monitor the work of the 10th Sabotage, having been given an order by Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, they know, perhaps through certain proposals to use the unit, and they have influenced the engagement of that unit. So the control of the unit is also possible because they are responsible for this unit professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "they are responsible for this unit professionally speaking," who do you mean? Who is the top person in intel and security who would be professionally responsible for the unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The chief. The chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this case, would be who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would be responsible for Salapura and his use or control of the 10th Sabotage?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the professional part. Of course, the first superior of the Colonel Salapura is Major-General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Another box that you've got and we have down here is the 65th Protection Regiment. Can you tell us a bit about that and where it fits.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When it is about issuing orders, it is related to the commander. Bearing in mind the structure and tasks, by that I mean to say that it is in charge of protection of the command post and the commander when it is stationary and when he is on the way, it also contains a battalion of military police. The security administration contains a department which is in charge for the work of the military police. We can say that it is actually a military department. But if we wanted to phrase it in a more precise way, we would say, department in charge of the military police affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And remind us who that would be in the security administration.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought you said it was the security department that oversaw the military police.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the administration -- of the security administration is Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you know where that military police unit for the 65th Protection Regiment was located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The regiment had two locations, I think. It was deployed in two locations. Those parts that provided security for the Main Staff were in the area of the Main Staff and the command. Some other parts of it were, I think, in Zalukovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us who the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment was in July, if you recall, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And one other department, you've noted it as department for civil affairs, we see it up at the top of ours connected to -- well, like all the rest, General Mladic, can you tell us what the -- what the department of civil affairs, just fundamentally, did? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a sector; it was a department. In charge of the liaison with the foreign military representatives and various other organisations. They were in charge of receiving information on the movement of various UNPROFOR convoys, convoys with the humanitarian aid, and, generally, for the contact with the peace force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you gave us, I believe, two names. Can you tell us who -- who was in charge of that unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This department was headed by Colonel Milos Djurdjic. Another person who was with him in that same department was Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Kralj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just to complete this -- the diagram, I -- let me just briefly go over the corps and get their names for -- to see if you agree. And the 1st Krajina Corps was commanded by Momir Talic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Will you know the ranks of the corps commanders? General, I'm sorry to spring that on you, but that is, of course, an important topic today. If not, don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Talic was lieutenant-colonel general at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the 2nd Krajina Corps, Radivoje Tomanic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Eastern Bosnia Corps, Novica Simic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major-General Novica Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the first part of July, 1995, Milenko Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And his rank?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was retired as a lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Drina Corps, after Zivanovic, Radislav Krstic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also, Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was commanded first by Stanislav Galic and later on by Major-General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the rank of Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-general, if I remember it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Herzegovina Corps, Radovan Grubac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General Radovan Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall anyone associated with the air force and anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The air force and anti-aircraft defence was commanded by Major-General Zivomere Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the military school centre, we see Rajko Balic [phoen] and Grujo Boric.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Major-General Grujo Boric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Balic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Balic also associated with the military school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you misspoke, Mr. McCloskey. I see in this sheet "Rajko Balac."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the school was Rajko Balac, after colonel who commanded the school and was killed, in the west. So the school got its name after him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. And then the box of the 1st Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was Lieutenant-Colonel Lalovic. But I'm not sure, when we talk about the relevant time that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what was this, very briefly, the 1st Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Guards Brigade is a unit attached to the staff. However, for the whole duration of the war, it was resubordinated to the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get those corrections done, Mr. President, and out to everyone reflecting the witness's testimony. And, General, you -- going to another topic. You testified previously about the importance of military reporting from both -- well, the brigades up to the corps, the corps to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff to the Supreme Command. And I, first of all, wanted to ask you about: Was there an order related to an oral reporting requirement for one particular unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was an order related to the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. To avoid writing written operative reports, they were told that they should get in touch at certain predefined times in the morning and in the evening to General Miletic. I think that that is the order that you showed me in my previous testimony. I don't know the exact number and I don't know exactly who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we see 65 ter 7260.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, we see an order. And we see that it comes from Commander Milomir Savcic, and I won't go over it all, but it basically says that: "Based on a verbal order of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff ... that in the future regular reports will not be written but the resident Chief of Staff will call Colonel Miletic on the telephone every day at 0800 hours and 1900 hours." Is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you showed me when I testified in that other case. So the regiment commander is instructed to report orally, and this is also referenced to the oral, verbal order by the chief of the Main Staff, instead of sending in a written report. And also they are told at which time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we also go to 65 ... yes, I would offer this in evidence. Thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we're here, can we go to exhibit -- 65 ter 5679.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we had just talked briefly about the 10th Sabotage Detachment and you'd said it was connected professionally to the intelligence unit. And we see here on 21 December 1994 from the Main Staff from -- it says the chief, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir, and it's entitled: "Warning re: The selection of the candidates for the Main Staff of the VRS of the 10th Sabotage Detachment." Is this the same 10th Sabotage Detachment that you spoke of earlier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we should clear just one word. Because you said that it was "attached." It wasn't really attached. They are simply talking about this professional line in relation to the selection of the personnel for this unit. That's the professional part for which it was the administration. It was an administration which was in charge of that part, and by that I mean particularly a selection of the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in English the term "attached" and "resubordinated" are two different military terms that have a formal military significance and sometimes it gets translated that way. And apparently the General just heard one of the formal military terms that I may have -- may have been translated. So that's where that's coming from. But I hope you understand what he's talking -- this professional connection that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see General Tolimir warning the -- whoever he is sending this to, which is not precisely clear, that he wants people to select candidates for this unit. Is General Tolimir's communication to the people to select candidates for this unit, is that consistent with his professional control over the unit that you've talked about, as opposed to the command of the unit, which you've made clear was Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The mobilisation and the manning, manning is within the jurisdiction of the sector for mobilisation and personnel, they have a department in charge of mobilisation and personnel within the sector. So it is possible to draw their attention to what kind of personnel they should accept. I don't see here to whom this document was sent, so what I just said was simply an assumption of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is General Tolimir acting within his responsibility in this document, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. It was the proposal of the chief of the administration for intelligence affairs, which contained the suggestion about what kind of personnel should be selected for this unit. And now he is sending a memo saying what should be borne in mind while selecting the personnel for this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you just tell us, generally, how important, if it is, is receiving reports from subordinate units to the Main Staff? For example, receiving reports on what's going on in their area of responsibility from the corps to the Main Staff. How important is this and why?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Reporting in the military is a very important thing because it is on the basis of a timely and accurate report that the superior command can react in an appropriate way to certain events. If the reports are inaccurate, then the decisions themselves are going to be wrong or inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at 65 ter 7259.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I offer this into evidence as well. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know -- take a minute to look at it. I think you were shown this before. It should have been in your packet. But we can see that it is from the Main Staff, dated 21 June 1994. And we -- I can tell that you that, from the second page, it is from the Chief of Staff, Manojlo Milovanovic. In fact, why don't we just show you the second page so you can see that in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
