utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the first page now. In the B/C/S too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see from the title of this report that it's regarding the poor utility of regular combat reports. It's issued to all the corps that you've just gone over. And we can see the criticisms. Paragraph 2, that it's below the level of the commands. And the second paragraph in paragraph 2 says: "The Main Staff and the Supreme Command can make no use, for the purpose of taking strategic decisions and waging the war, of information which states only how many rifle grenades or bullets the enemy fired at our forces." And then it goes on to further criticise it. Now, can you tell us -- we know who the Main Staff is, now can you tell us what is -- who is this Supreme Command? What is that a reference to, in 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Commander is the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic, and the state organs that -- of which the Supreme Command was composed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we see the next paragraph. It says: "The Main Staff requires, under item 1, (the enemy), the following information on the enemy: ... information on any enemy combat activity on a larger scale, information on the enemy's future intentions, information on the objective of forthcoming actions, ... information on the possibility of the enemy attaining the objectives of his forthcoming actions." Now, that information of the enemy, what branch normally is collecting information on the enemy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's the security and intelligence administration. It's the intelligence people that collect information about the enemy, the area where combat operations take place, the time, and the armed forces. The combat deployment, the grouping, the means of support of the enemy are analysed. What kind of engineering support they have or whatever else they have by services. In a word, everything that may be important for decision-making and the intentions of the enemy. All this information must be part of the daily operative report under item 1 and be forwarded to all subordinate units. Since our manning was at a low level and we didn't have trained personnel, there were some weaknesses. There were some shortcomings, such as these pointed out here by General Milovanovic in this warning, and there were even inaccuracies. Corps commanders informed the commander of the Main Staff in the afternoon or the evening, and in the report, the corps commander requests for permission to take out a day or two of leave; whereas in the report, it's stated that the commander was present, although, we at the Main Staff knew that the corps commander was absent at that point in time. It would happen frequently that the subordinate commanders sometimes would deliberately fail to faithfully depict the situation which was bad for them because they lost a certain area or they failed in their activities so they would only report about it a day or two later. Sometimes it was deliberate. Other times it was because the personnel in question was not properly trained to do the particular -- their particular jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Milovanovic suggests, in the paragraph 2, the second paragraph in paragraph 2, that -- that it's from these corps reports that the Main Staff and the Supreme Command may make strategic decisions on the waging of war. Is that -- is that correct? Is accurate information from the corps important for the strategic decisions that the Main Staff and the -- and President Karadzic make?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the accuracy of information and forecasts are one thing, and counting the shells that landed are -- is -- is a task for journalists. Professional soldiers are supposed to infer the enemy's intentions for the coming period from their past actions and inform the superior command about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the availability of a major unit, combat unit, having finished up one task and being ready for another, would that be the kind of information that would be important for the Main Staff to know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, for example, let's use the 10th Sabotage Detachment. If it was done with one of its operations and there was a need someplace else in the -- in the battle-front to use them, would the Main Staff need to know that the 10th Sabotage was available?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff must know because it's their unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that? Why must they know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Main Staff must know because it's a unit that is directly linked to the command of the Main Staff. No one corps can say, I'll take the sabotage detachment and use it here or there; they can only request the assistance of a unit that belongs to another formation or the Main Staff. And then that request can either be approved or not approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to offer that into evidence, that last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 65 ter 7259 will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go to P1215.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, this should be -- I'm not sure you've seen this, but I wanted to show you an example of -- of a report from the Main Staff to the president of the Republika Srpska. And before we look into this document, can you explain how that worked? We've seen General Milovanovic say that those daily combat reports from the corps had to be accurate. Did the Main Staff have a reporting requirement from the Main Staff to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: There's reporting from all levels upward. In the zone of responsibility of the corps, the brigades that are subordinated to the corps at certain time intervals, after 16- or 1700 hours, draft a report about the current situation and send them to the corps. At the corps level, all these brigade reports are integrated into one report which gives a snap-shot of the situation at 1800 hours and forward that to the Main Staff. The Main Staff, based on all reports received from the 1st Corps, 2nd Corps, Eastern Bosnian Corps, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Herzegovina Corps, military school centre, et cetera, integrates all these reports and forwards them to the president, or the supreme commander actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us what part of the Main Staff collects this information from the corps and puts it into a report to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If we had had an operations centre, that would be the body who was supposed to do it. But we didn't have one, so these would -- this information would come to us, to General Miletic's sector, and we would integrate the -- all these reports and forward them to the Chief of Staff. All these reports that went to the supreme commander we also copied to the corps commands so that they be aware of the situation in the entire theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last page of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe it's page 4. It's the signature page. Yes. I believe it should be page 4 in the B/C/S as well -- yes, I've got a -- you've got them both up there. I just want to concentrate on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all we see some initials. Not sure the interpreter could make out the initials on the original, or the B/C/S. Do you see those initials that are right before the signature line? I think it's "R Dj."

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Overlapping speakers] ... I only read --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: These are my initials and the initials of the person who typed up this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the left side of the left bottom part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be enlarged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, can you -- now, this is dated 12 July, this document, and the initials seem to be --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: If it's OLJ, then it's me. But I wasn't at the Main Staff on the 12th. So it may be another date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we do see the initials of R D, or Dj, I believe, is what it's called.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then it's Krsto Djeric. You showed me a document with my initials, OLJ. But this must be Krsto Djeric then, and the typist is MM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... we may have a glitch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- this abbreviation be enlarged again. For a short moment we could see that. So, sir, can you -- only the first letters, could you explain again what you see now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] M and Dj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this should be who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't reconstruct it now. M Dj. Djeric's name is Krsto, but this is M. Oh, yes, it's Mihajlo Djurdjevic [Realtime translation read in error "Mihajlovic Djordjevic"] from the engineers organ from the Staff. Mihajlo Djurdjevic, colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see it says, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff, Major-General Radivoje Miletic." Now, we spent a lot of time in the last trial about this issue. I think if can you -- can you just --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, can you explain what "standing in" means in the formal military sense? And then explain whether or not in your view General Miletic was actually standing in, as it suggests here, or whether it was something else.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, to stand in, strictly speaking and under the Law on the Army of former Yugoslavia, the person who stands in for somebody has all the powers of the establishment position in which he is at the moment, from the status of the level at the payroll, any benefits, et cetera, all the way through the power to impose sanctions or decide about incentives. And a person who stands in for somebody usually does so because the other is absent due to illness or for any other reason unable to perform his duties. In order to stand in for somebody, you must have an order to stand in. You may remember that at the beginning I mentioned some details from my biography. I said that in Derventa I was Chief of Staff and that I stood in for the commander. The commander was not appointed. And I performed both duties. I had the status elements of the commander while I was standing in for him. Here, General Miletic signed as the person standing in for the Chief of Staff, but he didn't actually stand in for the Chief of Staff who was in the Republika Srpska and actively participated in tackling some issues in the theatre of war. So this is wrong. He did not have the powers that go with the establishment position of Chief of Staff. In my previous testimony I said that I roughly know when that juncture was and when General Miletic starting signing as the person standing in for the Chief of Staff. If necessary, I can explain further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a short moment. In page 52, line 1, it is not properly recorded the name of the drafter of this document. If I understood you correctly. It was "Mihajlovic Djordjevic"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Mihajlo Djurdjevic. It is not "Djordjevic," Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is what I said. "Djurdjevic," with a U. It was not recorded properly. I have -- again it's not correct. I would like to have the name corrected on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's an E instead of the O in the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you just spell it out and we'll get it right once. That should fix it. Can you just spell it, the last name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: D-j-u-r-d-j-e-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've just asked if you should explain how this standing started being used in this important Main Staff report and you'll agree with me that it was used quite a bit. I mean, many we've seen, perhaps even hundreds, of these reports, where it says "standing in." Can you tell us how it started getting used and what it means in this context? You've described to us the formal process of standing in.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When I was with General Milovanovic at the forward command post, in the west of the Republika Srpska, Drvar more precisely, he, that is, General Milovanovic, invited General Jovo Maric and me to coffee in the morning. Such a report was on the table, a report which was sent to the supreme commander. And at one point he said, Why is this Mico fucking with me? I apologise. I send a report to myself, because in the signature block when things are sent coded, it said "Chief of Staff, General Manojlo Milovanovic." After that time, this started appearing. And when I came to Crna Rijeka, they always used this signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this job of assembling all this critical information and getting it up to the president would have been Milovanovic's job, had he been there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The reports don't only contain information about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just talking generally. These reports, had Milovanovic been at the Main Staff in 1995, he would have done this, not Miletic; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: No. We from the administration wrote -- drafted it and Milovanovic only reviewed it and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But reviewing it is rather important, as you've told us. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But he was kind of precise about it. He paid much attention to detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so the review and the signing off on these imports is an example of something that Miletic was doing while Milovanovic was away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's go to one of these -- another --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'd offer this into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's go to 65 ter 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this is the next day. And the same report from the Main Staff - it's the 13th July now - to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we can go to the last page. It should be 3, I believe, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't on page three in Serbian. Now we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So again we see, "standing in," and then General Miletic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let's -- let's go back to the front page now in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- I just want to, again pretty briefly -- we can see that it entitled "situation on the front line," and then it starts on this page with the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps. Then we go over to the next page. And we go down through the corps until we get --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could have page 3 in the English. And it's paragraph 6 in the B/C/S. Yes, we get to the DK, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to go over this briefly. As we see, under -- the part about the enemy, and the third sentence says: "The enemy from the former enclave of Srebrenica is in a state of total disarray and the troops are surrendering in large numbers to the VRS. A 200- to 300-strong group of soldiers managed to break through to the general sector of Mount Udrc ... where they are trying to break through to the territory under Muslim control." Skipping down a little bit to section (b): "The situation in the corps. Combat groups from other corps units are in the final stages of preparations aimed at settling the issue of the Zepa enclave." And then: "Situation in the territory. There's an organised and planned transfer of the population from Srebrenica to the territory under Muslim control." Okay. Now, we know you're not back yet to the Main Staff, so I'm not going to ask you about these facts, but I just want to call everyone's attention to the paragraphs I just read, specifically the remark about "total disarray" and "breakthrough to the sector of Mount Urdc" and "the Zepa enclave" and "the transfer of the population."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now if we could go to -- I'd offer that into evidence, if it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness: We see here again an abbreviation, NT. And then an abbreviation for the typist. Do you know who that could be, NT? If that is a correct translation in the English. Yes, it is NT. Do you know who is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's Nikola Trkulja [phoen]. I believe that his first name was Nikola. He was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to P1601 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you'll agree with me that this is a Drina Corps daily combat report to the Main Staff for that same day as the -- the last day, and so according to what you've told us this would one of the things you guys would be incorporating into your report to the president. And so I'd ask you to look at, under -- it should be the third paragraph under "the enemy." And I won't read it all out but I'll briefly go over these -- the points that I hope we remember from the last document. And it states: "The enemy from the former Srebrenica enclave are in total disarray and have been surrendering to the VRS in great numbers." And then it says: "One group of 200 to 300 enemy soldiers managed to cross over into the general Mount Urdc sector with a view to getting onto the territory under BiH control, BH control." Then in combat readiness, the last sentence of that first paragraph talks about combat groups from the other corps units are carrying out last preparations for resolving the issue of Zepa. And then under "situation" it talks about so far the transport of 15.000 Muslims from Potocari to Kladanj has been organised. Those are the same four points, as I entitled, disarray, Mount Urdc, Zepa, and the transport, that we saw going out to the president. Is that part of how this was done? You would take the information from the corps and put it into the report to the president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was taken over from a Drina Corps report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness should be asked whether he was in a position to see this document. He was not a member of the Main Staff when this document was issued. This document was issued on the 30th of July, 1995, when he was not in the Main Staff. So the Prosecutor should ask him whether he was, indeed, in a position to see this document at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Firstly I note that there was a mistranslation, I think. It's not the 30th of July, but the 13th of July. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think you'll recall, Mr. President, I acknowledged that, and the witness agreed with me, that he was not yet back until the 17th. And so we're just going over this in the context of how the reports are done and whether or not this is the way to do it. Yes, I am using these date, but I'm not -- as I think I've said, I'm not going to be asking you about this information because you weren't back yet. That's exactly -- well, close to what I said. I'm not sure where I said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I understand the situation, but I think we've covered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in this Drina Corps report there's also a mention that: "In Konjevic Polje and also in Nova Kasaba reception of Muslim civilians and soldiers who surrender is being carried out and [sic] taken in an organised fashion." Now I didn't -- as -- I don't recall, and I'm -- that that part about civilians being at that location was not mentioned in the report from the Main Staff to the president. Is it possible to mention all the details to the president? Is this a choice that is being made, in your view?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. We would have to go back to that document. Maybe there is a bullet point covering the situation on the territory. We would have to go back to the combined report by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is back -- oh, it has a number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And it's that third page in the English, and paragraph 6 in the B/C/S, under "Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is situation on the territory. And it says here: "There is an organised and planned transfer of the population from Srebrenica to the territory under Muslim control."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, that -- correct, and I agree with you. And that was -- was noted in the other report. But the -- the section that I -- I pointed out that was not noted was that civilians and soldiers were showing up in the area of Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba. That is not anywhere mentioned under the section of the Drina Corps. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I would agree. It is not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But on that -- on that topic, let's go to another document, where we just were. The 12th of July document, from the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was P1215.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it should be -- it's under, again, paragraph 6 for the -- under the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I would take us down to the bottom of the paragraph under the Drina Corps. And this one says: "The enemy has been attempting to withdrew from the Srebrenica enclave with women and children in the direction of Ravni Buljin and Konjevic Polje." So in this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please help us to find the relevant part. And it should be enlarged, please, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's at page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 3 and enlarge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's that last sentence on page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, we see here in the day prior's report, your main -- or the Main Staff report to the president, there is a reference to women and children heading in the direction of Konjevic Polje, and it's the next day's report where they actually reported arriving. So we do see it mentioned in this -- in this report, I guess, don't we?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we do not -- the collection does not contain the Drina Corps daily combat report from the 12th of July, so -- otherwise, I would go look at it, but we don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, last time you told us that at the Main Staff there was normally a morning briefing. Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When the commander was present at the Main Staff or when the Chief of Staff needed to have a briefing, then we would have a morning briefing. If not, then we would do it for ourselves in the staff sector every morning. The formal ones took place from time to time on a -- a -- as required. The formal ones were attended by chiefs of sectors and heads of administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get in a little more detail on this topic. But from the 17th, after you arrived, did you pretty much stay at the Crna Rijeka office and bedroom there near the office throughout the rest of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I resided and worked at the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did General Miletic reside and work at the same place during that same time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of us were like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I -- you also told the Court last time about some communications issues. You were asked about whether or not Milovanovic and Mladic were able to have contact while Milovanovic was out on the -- the western front, as it's been referred to, during this -- during July. Were they -- did they have contact, as far as you know, in some manner?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the forward command post we organised all types of communications that existed in the -- at the main command post. However, they are somewhat less developed. There was also a direct encrypted link by the 63 device. And the commander would call us from time to time to check what was happening in the area of the 2nd Corps and in the west. On several occasions, when General Milovanovic was not back from the field, I had an opportunity to report to the command of the Main Staff, although we wrote reports to the Main Staff from the former -- forward command post in the same way as the corps did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just try to clarify some of that. You mentioned, I think, a device. Something about 63. Can you tell us what that -- just that device is? They may not have heard everything you said.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's an encryption device which was made in 1963. That was the year of its make. It is installed on a telephone line thereby making that telephone line and connections established by it protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you referred to that as KZU 63?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the abbreviation, which stands for the cryptic protection device dash 63, or encryption device, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that encrypting the oral communications over the telephone, or was it some kind of encrypted fax thing over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Both were coded. If you used encryption, you had to use relay communications installed on telephones. Many people are confused by that. They think if you use a wire correction it must be protected, but that's not the case. You have to use the device in order to be fully protected. If you did not use encryption, then your conversations could be listened in, and that's why we have so many intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, you've been shown a few intercepted conversation in the last trial, and we'll get so some of those. And that's why I'm asking about this. So this encryption is for voice communications over the phone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was -- were you able to communicate from Crna Rijeka out to General Milanovic -- excuse me, Milovanovic with this machine so you could speak secure voice to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, we had all types of communications as in the main command post. However, only one line was protected. So our voice communication was protected and we could talk freely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. One last exhibit on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have 65 -- excuse me, it should be P400A in the English and I would think B in the B/C/S. Sorry, we don't need to do that anymore. Okay, just 400A. And, for the record, as the Court is aware, the -- the dates are not -- on -- on this part of the -- the transcript, so this is from 17 July at 1950 hours between Krstic and Commander and, in parentheses, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if you're back at the Main Staff by 1950 hours that evening? Are you at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, just in looking at this intercept, Krstic and Mladic, which Krstic would this be, in your view, if this is a genuine intercept?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Only the Drina Corps commander had that family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall that General Krstic, on the 17th of July, was the -- leading the Drina Corps in the attacks on the Muslim forces defending the Zepa enclave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you learn it shortly after arriving on the 17th? As you know, this campaign went on for at least another -- well, at least through the beginning of August --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what I want to ask you about -- well, Mladic says: "Krle, can you hear me?" Do you know General Krstic's nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then Mladic -- and Krstic then says: "I can hear you." Mladic says: "Full steam ahead." Krstic says: "Understood." Mladic says: "Get in touch with Miletic on the secure line, full steam ahead. I didn't accept the Turks' conditions." So if General Krstic was in the field in the Zepa area, would he have been able to use this security line that you've talked to [sic] in order to contact Miletic who was at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I could only speculate. I am not aware either of Krstic's or Mladic's positions. I don't know where they were. However, the meaning of this is that he should talk to Miletic on a protected line so the information is not leaked. I don't know why. It is not specified in here. But did he say, "Full steam ahead; keep up."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we're past the break and so it's a good time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed. We should have our second break now, and we'll resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you'll remember from last time you were asked about Main Staff Extension 155. We see that in intercepts and in other documents. Can you tell us, did -- was there an Extension 155 somewhere at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us where or whose extension it was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was the extension of the Chief of Staff. But on the same line there was another telephone which was situated in our room. It was a small room nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be the operations room is I think what you called it last time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The operative -- the operations room, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was using the Chief of Staff's office and that extension while Milovanovic was away? And I'm talking about the period after you got back, 17 July.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody used it. Nobody used that room. It was simply a sort of a living-room and also a sleeping room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who would pick up on Extension 155?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The chief would pick it up. And if he was absent, he would then transfer the line to the telephone in the operations room so that we could know if somebody called and then we would inform him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was in the operations room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Most often it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He had his own room. It was an office and a room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his extension number?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was General Miletic's nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Some among the people who were of his own rank used to call him Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about for General Tolimir? What would those that could -- or those among his own rank or higher, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Quite often we would address him as Toso, the commander and also some other people who were in a position to afford something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also last time you spoke a bit about the directives. And I think earlier in the day you said that that was one of the commander's jobs, to make directives. And we'll be looking at Directive 7 in particular. But before we get there, can you tell us what a -- from your experience in the Main Staff, what were these directives? We -- we see several of them up to Directive 7 and I believe there will was a couple after that. But what -- what is a directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: A directive is an act of command used by the highest echelons of command. A directive gives long-term tasks and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who normally or in your experience was authored or signed off on -- on these directives?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The directives were signed by the supreme commander and the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we've seen in Directive 7, for example, that it says at the end, "drafted by Miletic." Can you tell us who drafts these things and how that process happens?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The process of drafting a directive is carried out in accordance with the instruction on the work of commands and staffs. It uses a certain methodology. You can have a full or complete method of work, an abridged method of work, or a method of work which is called work without consulting the organs and commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know which method of work was used for Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The full or complete method.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you explain the process of how a directive is -- is drafted, how it's put together?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The basis for drafting the Directive number 7 was the analysis of combat readiness of the Bosnian Serb army which was carried out for the previous year. This analysis was completed at the end of January 1995. The following took place -- took part in this analysis: The commander of the Main Staff, as the presiding officer. He opens the discussion and then the corps commanders give their briefing, followed by chiefs of sectors of the Main Staff. And during the analysis conclusions are made related to the level of the accomplishment of the tasks defined for the previous year. And then they proceed to define the tasks for the following year. And it is on the basis of this that the commander formulates the basic principle, or the idea, after which all command organs perform their assessments, put forward their proposals, which are submitted to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: He then adopts the proposals, and those adopted proposals are then unified into a single body by the operative organ. So, the part that pertains to the enemy is the part that is processed and then proposed as the finalized product by the intelligence organ. From the basic idea to the defining of the combat task and all in between is defined by the staff. By that I mean to say that the proposals for the use of corps and subordinated units are put forward by the operations sector. And whatever pertains to the arms is put forward by the organs in charge of arms. And all is then unified into a document that constitutes a directive. The communications organ is going to work out the communications. The artillery organ, the artillery. And the anti-biological, nuclear, and chemical measures are going to be processed by the appropriate organ. Motorised units will be defined by the motorised artillery sector. And all these elements are then unified by the operations and training sector, after which it is submitted for the signature to the appropriate commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that if we take into account the official translation that we have, we now face a signal problem and I think we should clarify it. For example, page 69, line 6 [in English]: Organs in charge of arms. [Interpretation] Now we have something translated as organs in charge of arms as weapons, while he meant to say arms as arms of land forces. I have noticed that this particular word, "arms," of armed forces, is translated and interpreted in various ways in the transcript. I'm trying to draw your attention to the terminological confusion. The witness has simply said what he said. But I think that the interpretation into English that we received is something that needs to be further clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I heard the word "arms" in the interpretation in English. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think they're doing a pretty good job. I'm not sure in particular where I can fix any of that, so if there's -- but I, of course, will work with Mr. Gajic and -- and the transcript on -- on some of these issues because it's not always clear when you're standing here what's -- what's essential and what isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript will be checked at a later stage in comparison to the tapes, and I hope during the process of reviewing the transcript there may be a clarification in this respect. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You ended with that all these materials from the relevant organs and people are unified by the operations and training sector and would that -- that's General Miletic and you and the two other -- well, fundamentally who is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: There was also Colonel Krsto Djeric in that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so is it you -- you three that worked on unifying all these -- these different elements for this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to clarify something. I've explained the general process of making a directive; however, I haven't took part in drafting of any of the directives in the Main Staff. I didn't take part in any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, General, for clarifying that. Because we know you were not around there in March 17th, in that period. Do you know, have -- let me tell you, did you -- were you able to see Directive 7 after you got back on the 17th of July at some point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite by accident that I had to get something from the closet of General Miletic. And that's when I saw it and I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I believe last time you said you got it from his strong-box. I don't know how that's translated. But was there some sort of a locked cabinet or box where you were able to get Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It's a metal closet and General Miletic was in the possession of its key. I needed to take something else from it at the time, and that's when I saw this document and I simply browsed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know -- in your absence, General Miletic was present in March; his name is on it as "drafted by." Do you know who would have helped him back in those days, around March, when this thing was drafted and signed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was from other sectors who drafted their representative parts of this document. I forgot to tell you one thing a moment ago. For instance, the logistics support was one item in the directive, but it was most often done by the operations/logistics organ. However, the chiefs of services would definitely take part in wording the items that would affect their services. Logistics support, traffic service, infirmary, anything that would come within the purview of their sector within the logistics. So I don't know exactly who took part in drafting the Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have translated for us something called the operations logistic organ. What is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That's a sector for logistical support. Part of it was operations logistics organ, then chief of the technical service, then chief of the quartermaster service, then chief of the medical service, then there was also the veterinary service. So all these things come within the purview of the logistics support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I just wanted to make sure that the operations logistics is separate from the operations and training branch that you're from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's within the logistics sector. That's where you can find the operative logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I understand, as you've described it, that all these other organs contributed to this document. But I was just -- the people that unified it under General Miletic's drafting is what I was interested in. Since you weren't there, do you know, besides General Miletic, who worked on the drafting of the -- the unification of the drafting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But you can see in the directive that it was drafted by General Miletic and typed out, if I'm correct, by Z ... and I forgot the other letter. It usually contains the initials. Or maybe, in this case, the full name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's -- I think it's a good time to get this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Should be Exhibit P1214. Now, I think the B/C/S version has to be -- B/C/S in page 23 in e-court because there's a cover letter that I think somehow got put in the back of the B/C/S version. So could we see if page 23, the last part, of the B/C/S version I'm hoping is this cover letter. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, is this -- is this a cover letter that -- that went out with Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by the contents. It is signed by the Chief of Staff. And the cover letter was dictated by Krsto Djeric. I don't know who the typist may have been. The initials are SZ. Then there's the stamp of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, confirming the reception on the 21st of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So should the other corps have received an identical copy of -- of Directive 7 just, perhaps, with different cover letters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the cover letter had the same contents only the letterhead must have been different, that is, the address line. So whatever was sent to the 2nd Corps or the East Bosnia Corps must have had the same contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And drawing your attention to up in the left-hand corner under "very urgent," it says: "Directive for upcoming operations." So is this a directive for upcoming operations, like it says?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the one who processed it, Djeric, stated that. Basically it is about upcoming operations, but the serial number is 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that. And, in fact, since you mentioned numbers, let me ask you about this, the third line from the top of this, it's strictly confidential number 03/4 ... Does that 03/4 have any particular meaning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since Colonel Djeric is a member of the operations and training administration, he registered this document in the log-book of the operations and training administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is 03/4 a number indicating operations and training sector?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the /434. What's the last three digits mean, if anything?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That's the entry number for the document in that log-book, so it's number 4 -- 434.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the first page of Directive 7. I think we have it in the English. We just need to go back to where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we notice here the date of 8 March. The cover letter was March 17th but the actual document is dated 8 March. And it's from the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska. And you've told us that that involved Radovan Karadzic. And without going to the end, I can -- do you remember that this particular directive was signed off by Radovan Karadzic? And we'll get there in a minute.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get there. And we see that, like you've said, it's addressed to the -- to all the corps and some of the other area -- some of the other units we've talked about. And it's entitled: "Directive for further operations, OP point number 7." And it starts with: "The main characteristics of the international military and political situation." I don't want to get into that, but do you know what -- what branch of the Main Staff would have drafted this particular subject?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence administration and possibly the sector for morale would be the ones. But with emphasis on the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let's go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I wanted to add something. Since this is a directive by the supreme commander, possibly one of his organs, that is, organs of the republic, were involved in the assessment of the political situation, because this is both political and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think after we read this we can see that you're absolutely correct on that. But I don't -- we don't need to take time, for these purposes, to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get to the second paragraph. It should be number 3 in English. Actually, it's -- yeah. It's fine in English. And, yeah, now we see it on the -- it's entitled: "Muslim/Croat coalition forces." And it goes on and talks about the Federation forces and the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What branch would be putting in that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Since the intelligence organs at all levels are duty-bound to monitor or follow the activities of the enemy side constantly, the intelligence administration of the Main Staff collects information from its subordinate organs and analyses the information and, in this manner, drafts such a -- such a review, or such a presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 7 in the English. It's paragraph 3 in the B/C/S. Entitled: "The task of the Republika Srpska army." That's page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, if could you just skim over this, these -- this task, because I don't want to ask you about all these tasks, but I do want you to -- and I want everyone to get a little feel for what is in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we need to go on to the next page in English. And it's the last sentence before paragraph 4. And after listing a bunch of tasks, it says: "Number 4 ... create the optimum conditions for the state and political leadership to negotiate a peace agreement and accomplish the strategic objectives of the war ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this anticipate that -- that a peace agreement could actually happen this year, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably at that level, where the situation is assessed and conclusions are drawn from all peace talks. The tasks were taken from the analysis I was speaking about, based on the information and conclusions of the commanders for their own units. And then at this level this was integrated into a -- into more or less general or specific tasks. It is the duty of the army to create as favourable conditions as possible for politics to have a stronger stand in -- in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, back in July, was it -- was -- was there a feeling that this war was going to end, or what was the feeling in regarding of that? I mean, when we look at this, it's talking about a negotiated peace, but was that actually something that, at the time, you felt was realistic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can speak about myself. When I arrived and got some insight, the situation for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was very unfavorable because the Muslim side launched a general offensive and it went on pretty long. Later on I learned that some officers were sent to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The situation was bad at Mount Vlasic, then around Doboj. Not to speak about the 2nd Krajina Corps. The -- a difficult situation had prevailed for quite some time. And when I arrived there, I wasn't really an optimist. Not at all the way you are interpreting this. Or maybe this was drafted in an optimistic manner. Possibly at that point in time I had too little general knowledge to be an optimist and conclude that the end was near.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you what you said in the Popovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's at page 28344.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And since it's in English, I will -- I'll need to read this to you, and I would think it would be able to come up, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we need the document number. You only referred to a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one -- one second. I surprised myself with this, but we'll get -- get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if -- I believe Ms. Stewart will show this on Sanction so we can see this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would like to have the document number for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the transcript, and I don't think it has an actual number yet. But it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course not because this is a viva voce witness and therefore his testimony in that case is not part our documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- that's right. And I see the section we're looking -- I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But we see on the top of this page that it is the transcript of the testimony of Witness Ljubo Obradovic, in open session,

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we're repeating a little history and then it will be over tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I read you a section. And I'm not sure right now where that particular section is. I -- let me -- but let me read this again and I'll find it. But the section I read to you was, and I quote: "'And thus by force of arms impose the final outcome of the war on the enemy, forcing the world into recognizing the actual situation on the ground and ending the war.'" And then I asked you: "So it fair to say that the time this was written, the -- there was actually a belief that the war may end, that the planning for the end of the [sic] war is actually happening?" And you answer: "Yes." Now, of course, this is different from the paragraph I just read to you, so I'm sorry about that. Having that section I just read to you and seeing your answer, do you stand by your answer that you gave in the Popovic case? And, General, I'm sorry. Let me just interrupt you. I see the section that I just read. It was right above the one I actually read. So it's in that paragraph right above paragraph 4, as we can all -- well, we'll see if we go back to Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record again, you were reading the lines 15 through 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The beginning of your quotation was a quote from a different document, not part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, can we -- I'm sorry, can we go back to Directive 7. P1214.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look in that -- in the middle of the paragraph, before "-- I hereby decides [sic]," it says -- yeah, just before point 2. The section I read at trial is right there. So I'll read that. "'... inflict as much damage on his troops, equipment, and materiel as possible and thus by force of arms impose the final outcome of the war on the enemy, forcing the world into recognizing the actual situation on the ground and ending the war.'" What I read to you earlier today was the last sentence: "... to create an optimum conditions for the state and political leadership to negotiate a peace agreement and accomplish the strategic objectives of the war." Now, based on that paragraph and your answer to my previous question, one last answer, General, and we'll break for the evening, do you stand by what you said in Popovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I must explain. The beginning of this paragraph with all these activities listed, it begins: "In case of an end of a -- the four months' truce and a continuation of the war," and then it goes on, what should be done. But the condition for all that is that the four months' truce is interrupted and the war extended, or continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This would be a good time to break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We have to adjourn for today, and we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon; 2.15 in this courtroom. You should be reminded that it is not allowed to have contact with either party during the break, sir. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
